title: Why You Must Keep Teaching Until The Last Day Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the common instinct to ease off academics and standards as the school year winds down, insisting that any visible drop in urgency undermines everything a teacher has built over the year. His central claim is that when standards and expectations drop, misbehavior predictably rises "like day turns into night," and that easing off signals to students that the teacher's stated convictions about the importance of school were never fully sincere. He extends the argument to time itself, insisting every day carries equal weight — Friday afternoon as much as Monday morning, the day before a break as much as any other day — and that treating the calendar's end as a natural off-ramp damages both behavior and the teacher's credibility. He does allow for measured, time-limited celebrations and mementos like yearbook signing, but draws a firm line against letting academic rigor or behavioral expectations slide. The concrete claim closing the piece is that students who already love being part of an SCM classroom won't resent losing extra treats on the final day, because the relationship was never built on rewards in the first place.
points: Any visible drop in standards near year's end is said to trigger a predictable rise in misbehavior, "like day turns into night."
Easing off is framed as revealing that a teacher's stated convictions about school's importance were never fully sincere.
Every school day is treated as carrying equal urgency — Friday as much as Monday, the day before a break as much as any other.
Measured celebrations and yearbook signing are allowed, but academic rigor and behavioral expectations should never slide.
quotes: It doesn’t matter whether you have a week left in the school year or a single day, just like any other break, be it winter or spring, you must keep pushing the envelope.
Like day turns into night, when standards and expectations drop misbehavior increases.
Fair or not, it sends the message to your students that you really didn’t mean it.
Public schools are failing. They’re spiraling along with many private schools as well.
Be a leader whose impact resonates in the lives of your students for months, years, and decades later.
